```{r}
#| label: results-setup
#| include: false
#| eval: true

library(dplyr)

here::i_am("manuscript/main.qmd")

endemic_summary <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("figures", "endemic_scenario", "results_summary.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
targeting_summary <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("figures", "endemic_targeting", "results_summary.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

endemic_value <- function(archetype, efficacy, coverage, statistic) {
  rows <- endemic_summary |>
    filter(
      archetype == .env$archetype,
      efficacy == .env$efficacy,
      coverage == .env$coverage
    )
  if (nrow(rows) != 1L) {
    stop("Expected one endemic summary row")
  }
  rows |> pull(all_of(statistic))
}

targeting_value <- function(
  archetype,
  efficacy,
  coverage,
  coverage_type = "targeted_riskiness",
  metric = "incidence_reduction",
  statistic = "mean_value"
) {
  rows <- targeting_summary |>
    filter(
      archetype == .env$archetype,
      efficacy == .env$efficacy,
      coverage == .env$coverage,
      coverage_type == .env$coverage_type,
      metric == .env$metric
    )
  if (nrow(rows) != 1L) {
    stop("Expected one targeting summary row")
  }
  rows |> pull(all_of(statistic))
}

format_result <- function(value, digits = 1, scale = 1) {
  formatC(scale * value, format = "f", digits = digits)
}

# Ratios compare the same coverage/efficacy grid for both archetypes.
endemic_ratio_range <- function(statistic) {
  endemic_summary |>
    filter(coverage %in% c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8), efficacy %in% c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8)) |>
    select(archetype, coverage, efficacy, all_of(statistic)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
      names_from = archetype,
      values_from = all_of(statistic)
    ) |>
    summarise(low = min(flu / sars_cov_2), high = max(flu / sars_cov_2))
}

# Compare marginal means for the relative increase reported in the text.
targeting_relative_increase <- function(archetype, efficacy, coverage) {
  targeted <- targeting_value(archetype, efficacy, coverage)
  random <- targeting_value(archetype, efficacy, coverage, "random")
  (targeted - random) / random
}

epidemic_summary <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("figures", "epidemic_scenario", "results_summary.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    coverage = signif(coverage, 2),
    efficacy = signif(efficacy, 2)
  )

epidemic_baseline <- epidemic_summary |>
  filter(coverage == 0 | efficacy == 0) |>
  group_by(archetype, metric) |>
  summarise(
    mean_value = mean(mean_value),
    min_value = min(min_value),
    max_value = max(max_value),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

epidemic_baseline_value <- function(archetype, metric, statistic) {
  epidemic_baseline |>
    filter(archetype == .env$archetype, metric == .env$metric) |>
    pull(all_of(statistic))
}

epidemic_value <- function(
  archetype,
  metric,
  strategy,
  efficacy,
  coverage,
  statistic = "mean_value"
) {
  rows <- epidemic_summary |>
    filter(
      archetype == .env$archetype,
      metric == .env$metric,
      coverage_type == .env$strategy,
      efficacy == .env$efficacy,
      coverage == .env$coverage
    )
  if (nrow(rows) != 1L) {
    stop("Expected one epidemic summary row")
  }
  rows |> pull(all_of(statistic))
}

epidemic_reduction <- function(efficacy, coverage) {
  baseline <- epidemic_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.4, 0.4)
  value <- epidemic_value(
    "flu",
    "epidemic_final_size",
    "Random",
    efficacy,
    coverage
  )
  (baseline - value) / baseline
}
```

# Abstract {-}

Respiratory virus transmission occurs in indoor settings where ventilation, occupancy, and dwell time determine exposure levels.
Improving indoor air quality (IAQ) therefore could help reduce disease burden associated with respiratory viruses, yet its population-level impact remains poorly quantified.
Here, we develop an individual-based transmission modelling framework that uses the Wells–Riley equation to inform ventilation-related variation in transmission risk between locations.
We use this modelling approach to evaluate IAQ-improving interventions (air-quality interventions or AQIs) under hypothetical intervention efficacies, using endemic and pandemic pathogen archetypes with properties similar to SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A/B, and evaluate how effects on key epidemiological metrics (such as annualized incidence and epidemic final size) depend on AQI coverage, efficacy and allocation strategy.
In model projections at 20% AQI intervention coverage and an assumed 80% reduction in location-specific force of infection, annualized incidence was reduced by approximately `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% for the endemic SARS-CoV-2 archetype, and `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% for the endemic influenza A/B archetype; at 60% coverage (80% efficacy) the reductions were `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.6, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% and `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.6, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`%, respectively.
Targeting AQI installation to the highest-risk locations outperformed random allocation: for SARS-CoV-2 transmission, 20% coverage at 80% efficacy cut absolute incidence by `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% when targeted versus `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "random"), scale = 100)`% when random; for influenza A/B transmission, this comparison was `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% versus `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "random"), scale = 100)`%.
In epidemic scenarios, random installation at 40% coverage and 60% efficacy reduced final size by `r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "mean_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (influenza A/B) versus `r format_result(epidemic_value("sars_cov_2", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "mean_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (SARS-CoV-2).
These results highlight the potential for IAQ interventions to reduce respiratory infection burden, particularly through risk-based deployment.
Their value as public-health infrastructure will depend on real-world effectiveness, costs, implementation quality, and achievable coverage.

# Background

Respiratory infections remain among the leading causes of global morbidity and mortality across the life course.
Lower respiratory infections (LRIs) (predominantly pneumonia and bronchiolitis) account for over two million deaths worldwide each year, with substantial concentration of mortality in young children and older adults.
In 2021 alone, LRIs were estimated to cause approximately 2.18 million deaths, including approximately 502,000 in children under five [@lri2021burden].
Viral pathogens are major contributors to this burden: seasonal influenza is responsible for around a billion infections annually, including 3–5 million severe cases and an estimated 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths [@whoInfluenza]; respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) drives a heavy paediatric toll, causing approximately 3.6 million hospitalisations and approximately 100,000 deaths in children under five each year, the vast majority in low- and middle-income countries [@li2022global].
Endemic human coronaviruses (OC43, NL63, 229E, HKU1) account for a large proportion of experienced “common colds”, while rhinoviruses are a leading trigger of asthma and COPD exacerbations, adding substantially to healthcare use and disability [@wilson2024global; @kurai2013virusinduced].
Beyond human costs, these infections impose sizeable economic burdens through hospitalisations and productivity losses [@langer2024the].
Immunity is rarely sterilising: previous work has highlighted that reinfections are common across a wide range of respiratory pathogens, with individuals experiencing seasonal coronavirus infection approximately once every 2.5 years on average [@edridge2020seasonal], influenza infection rates approaching 40% annually in some populations [@cohen2021asymptomatic], and SARS-CoV-2 reinfection occurring within approximately a year of prior infection [@guedes2023reinfection; @ma2023trends].
This recurrent pattern of infection means that the cumulative burden of respiratory viral disease over the life course is substantial.

A large share of respiratory-virus transmission occurs indoors, across both households and the other settings in which individuals routinely spend a high proportion of their time and which involve sustained close proximal contact with other individuals (e.g. schools, workplaces etc.) [@ferretti2024digital].
Previous work has shown the household to be an important site of influenza virus transmission, with estimates suggesting as much as 38% of transmission might occur in households [@tsang2016household].
Work using COVID-19 contact tracing app data has highlighted that approximately 40% of COVID-19 transmission occurs in households, with the majority of other transmission occurring in settings recurrently visited outside the household [@ferretti2024digital].
Serological evidence from a Swiss cohort suggests around 28% of COVID-19 infections were attributable to household transmission.
A corollary of these studies is that a sizeable fraction of respiratory virus transmission occurs outside the household.
Indeed, evidence from population-level modelling of transmission rates across multiple European countries has demonstrated the role specifically of non-household settings in sustaining population-level spread; showing that closures of non-essential businesses and schools were associated with approximately 35% and 7% reductions in the reproduction number of COVID-19, respectively [@sharma2021understanding].
Relatedly, prior work has shown that closure of schools over holiday periods in France led to significant reductions in influenza incidence [@cauchemez2008estimating], whilst recent work examining smart thermometer data from US households has suggested as much as 70% of household viral transmission might be initiated by children infected outside of the household [@tseng2023smart].

Much of this transmission is thought to occur via inhalation of aerosolised virus transmitted over relatively long distances, rather than short distance transmission via direct exposure to droplets produced during symptoms such as sneezing and coughing.
Previous work has demonstrated the viability of exhaled SARS-CoV-2 aerosols for transmission [@alsved2023infectivity], as well as empirical evidence from COVID-19 superspreading events during the pandemic (e.g. the Skagit Valley choir superspreading event [@hamner2020high]) and mathematical modelling of closed populations on the Diamond Princess [@azimi2021mechanistic] have all highlighted the significance of aerosolised SARS-CoV-2 transmission.
Similar results for influenza have confirmed the presence of infectious virus in the exhaled breath of infected individuals [@yan2018infectious], and have suggested that as much as 50% of all transmission events may be attributable to aerosolised virus [@cowling2013aerosol].

Indoor transmission is driven, in part, by crowding and inadequate ventilation in the spaces where people spend most of their time.
These conditions increase the risk of respiratory virus transmission.
Although ANSI/ASHRAE Standard 62.1 sets minimum outdoor-air requirements and default occupant densities for common space types, real-world occupancy frequently exceeds design assumptions and the effective per-capita ventilation rate can drop sharply during busy periods [@ashraeStandards; @ASHRAE].
Previous studies have consistently identified substandard ventilation in schools for example [@daisey2003indoor], with measurements in recently constructed U.S. schools showing that only approximately 22% of classrooms met the recommended minimum ventilation rates [@batterman2017ventilation].
More broadly, previous work has highlighted that ventilation is also highly heterogeneous across setting types, and frequently insufficient.
Surveys and reviews report wide distributions of air changes per hour (ACH) in homes and offices [@persily2008ventilation; @nazaroff2021residential], and that many routinely occupied rooms operate with insufficient ventilation rates [@corsi22006ozone].
Moreover, these crowding and ventilation deficits are not evenly distributed.
Mobility-network analyses during COVID-19 show that disadvantaged groups tend to visit more crowded points of interest with higher modeled infection risk [@chang2021mobility].
The structure of the built environment and how and where individuals spend their time is therefore thought to be a key driver of socio-economic inequities in disease burden.
Evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic has shown that locations visited by disadvantaged racial and socioeconomic groups were, on average, more crowded and therefore associated with higher infection risk [@chang2021mobility], a factor in turn likely to be driving the disparities in infection rates observed in the US during the pandemic’s earliest months [@millett2020assessing].

Motivated by this, a growing literature is testing practical ways to improve indoor air quality (IAQ) and, in turn, reduce respiratory-virus exposure and burden across everyday settings.
Interventions aimed at achieving this goal typically span those increasing effective ventilation/air changes (such as upgrades to HVAC systems) [@who2021ventilation], portable particulate filtration (e.g. via HEPA filtration units) [@chen2022efficacy], and installation of technologies aiming to directly disinfect air (such as ultraviolet germicidal irradiation approaches including far-UVC 222nm) [@eadie2022faruvc].
Evidence supports the potential utility of these approaches.
Lab studies have highlighted the utility of upper room UV at limiting tuberculosis transmission [@escombe2009upperroom], and that far-UVC technologies can rapidly inactivate viral bioaerosols [@eadie2022faruvc].
Prior work in healthcare settings has similarly shown that portable HEPA filters with UV sterilisation can remove detectable airborne SARS-CoV-2 RNA from clinical wards [@conwaymorris2022the].
In schools, recent work has shown that incorporation of air purifiers was associated with a reduction in student absences of 12.5% [@bonan2025the], while other studies have highlighted associations between higher ventilation rates and decreased SARS-CoV-2 airborne transmission in school classrooms [@buonanno2022increasing] and college dormitories  [@gold2025impact].
Previous work has documented reduced ARI incidence in the intention-to-treat group during studies of air purifiers in residential aged care facilities [@thottiyilsultanmuhammedabdulkhadar2024air], and that germicidal UV light can similarly reduce ARI incidence in these settings [@shoubridge2025germicidal].

Despite this emerging evidence base, the majority of studies are empirical, device- and setting-specific, and frequently evaluate proximate outcomes (e.g., PM/CO$_2$ concentrations, pathogen RNA detection, absenteeism) within single rooms or facilities, and focus on local environments, short-horizon endpoints and specific populations.
As a result, we still lack a coherent framework to quantify how indoor air interventions might alter pathogen transmission dynamics and disease burden at the population level, and resolve their potential public-health impact under varying epidemiological conditions.
Doing so will be crucial in supporting rigorous, quantitative cost–benefit analyses, as well as supporting targeting of these interventions across the diverse setting types and locations in which they could potentially be deployed.
Motivated by this gap, we developed an individual-based epidemiological modelling framework that represents individuals’ membership of locations across different setting types (households, schools, workplaces, leisure, and community venues) and links them to within-room airborne transmission processes (ventilation, filtration, and UV inactivation).
This framework integrates time-use, occupancy, and airflows with pathogen emission, dispersion, and removal.
Using pathogen archetypes approximating SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A/B (hereafter referred to as SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A/B) as case studies, we simulate a range of indoor-air interventions, varying efficacy, coverage, and targeting across setting types under both endemic and pandemic scenarios to estimate effects on transmission, epidemic trajectories, and health burden.
Our model projections suggest substantial potential public-health benefits from improving indoor air quality, supporting further evaluation of “clean indoor air” as public-health infrastructure alongside vaccines and therapeutics.

# Methods

## Population structure and data sources

We simulated a population of individuals stratified into three age groups: children, adults, and elderly (@fig-population, panel A).
Household sizes (@fig-population, panel E) and age composition were sampled from a 2010 San Francisco-based synthetic population produced by RTI International [@rineer2025a].
School enrollment sizes (@fig-population, panel G) were sampled from U.S. National Center for Education Statistics 2019–2020 data [@deBrey2023Digest].
Workplace sizes (@fig-population, panel I) were sampled from a truncated offset power law distribution estimated previously from US-based data [@ferguson2005strategies].
In the absence of detailed data and information on visit frequency and duration to other settings, we aggregated all other visits into a “leisure” category, with setting capacity (@fig-population, panel C) and visit frequency (@fig-population, panel B) sampled from empirically motivated negative binomial and Poisson distributions respectively.

## Overview of individual-based modelling framework

We developed a stochastic, individual-based epidemiological model in which space is explicitly represented by assigning each individual to membership of particular locations and setting types, following the approach of Ferguson et al [@ferguson2005strategies].
In what follows, we use “setting type” to denote classes of place (e.g., households, schools, workplaces, leisure venues), and “location” to index a specific instance of a given setting type (e.g., a particular household, school, workplace or leisure venue).
Each location is represented as a single aggregate unit (i.e. without rooms within locations).

Within the model, individuals exist in one of several disease states: susceptible, exposed (but not yet infectious), infectious, and recovered.
Individuals progress through these states according to pathogen-specific natural history parameters, while acquisition of infection is governed by an exposure process that is computed based on the specific set of locations individuals visit during the course of a day.
At each time step, an individual’s total force of infection (FOI) is the sum of location-specific FOIs from the locations that they visit.
Individuals are assumed to visit different setting types depending on their age group.

For each location *j* belonging to setting type s, the force of infection experienced by an individual visiting that location is proportional to the fraction of visiting individuals in that location who are currently infectious.
This proportion is scaled by a setting-type specific transmissibility parameter ${\beta }_{s}$ and a location specific heterogeneity multiplier ${\gamma }_{j,\ s}$.
The former captures differences in respiratory virus transmission between setting types [@ferretti2024digital], while the latter captures variation in occupancy, ventilation, and mixing across locations of the same setting type and is parameterised using information on ventilation rates.
This construction lets us (i) control the average contribution of each setting type to transmission at the population level and (ii) represent between-location heterogeneity in transmission risk across the locations belonging to a particular setting type.
We do not explicitly represent the duration or sequence of individuals’ visits to locations.

To quantify between-location “riskiness”, we use empirically documented variation in ventilation rates across locations belonging to the same setting type, and integrate these with an explicit model of within-room airborne virus concentration and a Wells–Riley dose–response model.
This connects observed variation in ventilation to differences in transmission risk between locations, allowing us to assess how this heterogeneity affects population transmission and the benefits of targeting higher-risk locations.
We represent interventions as assumed proportional reductions in location-specific force of infection to compare efficacy, coverage, and allocation strategies; the efficacy achievable with specific ventilation, filtration, or disinfection must be established separately.
This framework (described in further detail below) is implemented in R as an open-source package [@helios], built using the *individual* R package; package documentation, vignettes, and source code are publicly available.
Further model details are provided below, but see [https://mrc-ide.github.io/helios/](https://mrc-ide.github.io/helios/) for full details.

## Transmission dynamics and calculation of individual force of infection

Following the approach of Ferguson et al [@ferguson2005strategies], the force of infection (FOI) experienced by an individual $i$ at time $t$ is decomposed across the location $j$ and setting type $s$ as follows
$${\lambda }_{i}\left({t}\right)=\sum\limits_{j,s}^{}{\lambda }_{i,j,s}\left({t}\right).$$

The location and setting type-specific FOI is calculated as

$${\lambda }_{i,j,s}\left({t}\right)=\frac{{\beta }_{j,s}{I}_{j,s}\left({t}\right)}{{N}_{j,s}},$$

where ${I}_{j,s}\left({t}\right)$ is the number of infectious individuals in location $j$ belonging to setting type $s$, ${N}_{j,s}$ is the occupancy in that particular location, and ${\beta }_{j,s}={\gamma }_{j,s}{\beta }_{s}$ is a transmissibility parameter.
The setting-specific transmissibility $\beta_s$ was parameterised to reflect empirical estimates of how influenza and SARS-CoV-2 transmission is apportioned between setting types.
The location-specific multiplier $\gamma_{j,s}$ captures heterogeneity in transmission risk between locations of the same setting type, informed by variation in ventilation rates and occupancy density.
These multipliers were drawn from a truncated lognormal distribution with log-mean zero and log-standard deviation $\sigma_{\log,s}$ (@fig-population, panels D, F, H, and J).
The ventilation-informed parameterisation of this distribution is described in @sec-location-riskiness.

We set between-setting transmission rate ratios based on estimates from prior work about how overall transmission is apportioned between settings [@ferretti2024digital; @Fergusonetal2006]

$${\beta }_{\mathrm{household}}:[{\beta }_{\mathrm{school}}\text{ or } {\beta }_{\mathrm{workplace}}]:{\beta }_{\mathrm{leisure}}:{\beta }_{\mathrm{community}}=30\%:30\%:30\%:10\%,$$

with ${\beta }_{\mathrm{school}}$ or ${\beta }_{\mathrm{workplace}}$ depending on the age-class an individual belongs to, and with the sum of ${\beta }_{s}$ values scaled to achieve overall levels of transmission consistent with reproduction number estimates for the specific pathogen archetypes modeled (see below).
Households, workplaces, schools and leisure settings are explicitly represented within the modelling framework; “community” transmission is used to represent residual infection risk occurring in locations or contexts outside these settings.

## Indoor air quality motivated variation in riskiness between locations {#sec-location-riskiness}

We used an airborne concentration model and the Wells–Riley dose–response equation to inform the variation in riskiness $\gamma_{j,s}$ between locations $j$ of the same setting type $s$.
Following @blatchley2023quantitative, we described airborne pathogen concentration $C(t)$ using the ordinary differential equation

$$\nu \frac{dC\left({t}\right)}{dt}=-QC\left({t}\right)-{k}_{\mathrm{D}}\nu C\left({t}\right)+I\pi ,$$

where $\nu$ is room volume, $Q$ is air flow rate, $I$ is the number of infectious occupants, ${k}_{\mathrm{D}}=0.64{h}^{-1}$ is a pathogen decay constant [@blatchley2023quantitative], and $\pi =27$ virions per person per hour is the emission rate [@blatchley2023quantitative].
We assumed room volume $\nu =N{D}_{s}H$ where $N$ is the maximum room occupancy, ${D}_{s}$ is floor area (${m}^{2}$) per person (${D}_{\mathrm{household}}=20$, ${D}_{\mathrm{school}}=3.33$, ${D}_{\mathrm{workplace}}=10$, ${D}_{\mathrm{leisure}}=2$ [@kelechava2022ventilation]), and $H=2.5m$ is the room height.
We evaluated the steady-state concentration for one infectious occupant ($I=1$),

$$C_{\mathrm{ss}}=\frac{\pi}{\nu(\mathrm{ACH}+k_{\mathrm{D}})},$$

where $\mathrm{ACH}=Q/\nu$ is the ventilation rate in air changes per hour.
For this concentration, the probability of infection for a susceptible individual exposed for dwell time $\tau$ is given by the Wells–Riley equation [@wellsAirborne; @riley1978airborne], as

$$P_i(\tau)=1-\exp\left({-rBC_{\mathrm{ss}}\tau}\right),$$

with breathing rate $B=0.45{m}^{3}{h}^{-1}$ and infection probability per virion $r=1.37\times {10}^{-2}$  [@blatchley2023quantitative; @killingley2022safety].
For each explicitly represented setting type, we evaluated the Wells–Riley infection probability across the ACH range reported in @corsi22006ozone, using dwell times of 12 hours in households, 8 hours in schools and workplaces, and 2.5 hours at leisure venues.
These dwell times are used only to parameterise between-location risk heterogeneity and do not specify individual visit durations in the population simulation.
Holding the other exposure parameters fixed, the minimum and maximum ACH gave the upper and lower infection-probability bounds, respectively.
The ratio of these probabilities (upper divided by lower) defined a setting-specific riskiness ratio $R_s$.
This ratio determined the bounds $[R_s^{-1/2}, R_s^{1/2}]$ of a median-one truncated lognormal distribution, with setting-specific log-standard deviation $\sigma_{\log,s}$ selected numerically to place approximately 80% of the distribution within $[(R_s/2)^{-1/2}, (R_s/2)^{1/2}]$ and 10% in each tail (see Supplementary Information).
Each location was assigned a fixed multiplier $\gamma_{j,s}$ drawn from this distribution, with changes in infection risk during the simulation driven by infectious occupancy through $I_{j,s}(t)/N_{j,s}$ rather than recalculated airborne concentrations or Wells–Riley probabilities.

## Modelling the impact of air quality interventions

We modeled the impact of generic air quality interventions (AQIs) that either modify the physical number of air changes per hour (ACH) or increase the rate at which exhaled virus becomes inactive (thereby decreasing the total virus concentration in a room, in what is typically referred to as the “effective air changes per hour” or eACH).
Given substantial heterogeneity between different AQIs in terms of changes to eACH and dependence on the specific ventilation dynamics of each space, as well as the initial, exploratory nature of this work, we made the simplifying assumption that modeled AQIs installed in a given setting would reduce the location-specific FOI multiplicatively by efficacy ${E}_{j,s}$ and modify the FOI as follows

$${\lambda }_{i,j,s}^{\mathrm{AQI}}\left({t}\right)=\left({1-{E}_{j,s}}\right)\times {\lambda }_{i,j,s}\left({t}\right).$$

With this formulation, we then carried out a suite of sensitivity analyses varying AQI efficacy, coverage level (i.e. the target proportion of combined eligible non-household floor area receiving AQI installation), and allocation strategy (randomly distributed across locations vs. targeted to highest-risk eligible locations).
AQIs were eligible for installation in schools, workplaces, and leisure venues; households and background community transmission were excluded.
Under targeted allocation, eligible locations were ranked by their location-specific riskiness multiplier $\gamma_{j,s}$, with AQIs installed in descending order until the cumulative covered floor area met or exceeded the coverage target.
We define highest-risk locations as those with the largest $\gamma_{j,s}$ values across these three setting types.

## Disease and AQI scenario modelling

We simulated two pathogen archetypes with epidemiological properties similar to those of influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2, including the natural history (average incubation period of 2 days and an average duration of infectiousness of 4 days for the SARS-CoV-2 pathogen; average incubation period of 1 day, average duration of infectiousness of 2 days for the influenza A/B pathogen), and reproduction number (approximately ${R}_{0}\approx 1.5$ for the influenza A/B pathogen and ${R}_{0}\approx 2.5$ for the SARS-CoV-2 pathogen).
For both pathogen archetypes, we carried out a suite of simulations assuming both endemic transmission (i.e. in which transmission is recurring and individuals are routinely reinfected due to declining immunity levels, and which matches the current dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A/B); and an alternative set of “epidemic” scenarios in which a novel pathogen with properties similar to those of influenza A/B or SARS-CoV-2 emerges into the population.

We simulated both endemic and epidemic scenarios for each pathogen archetype under multiple AQI strategies: no AQI (baseline), random allocation of AQI to locations, and targeted allocation to the highest-risk eligible locations.
Each scenario was replicated 25 times to account for stochastic variation between model runs.
For endemic scenarios, we computed annualized disease incidence and average prevalence of active infection over the time-period simulated.
Endemic simulations were run for 20 years with an assumed mean duration of immunity of 365 days, and interventions were introduced following the end of the 10th year, across indoor settings including workplaces, schools, and leisure venues.
The period spanning years 5–7 served as the baseline, and years 15–17 as the post-intervention phase for purposes of evaluation.
For epidemic scenarios, we computed epidemic final size and peak infection incidence as metrics to assess AQI impact.
Epidemic simulations were run for 4 years, with interventions introduced at the start of the simulation.

# Results

**AQI installation is projected to substantially reduce endemic respiratory virus infection incidence, depending on coverage and assumed efficacy.**
Across the explored scenarios, AQI installation reduced annualized disease incidence and the prevalence of active infections across both pathogen archetypes considered, though overall impact depended strongly on coverage (defined as the target proportion of non-household floor area receiving AQI installation) and the efficacy of the AQI (defined as the proportion reduction in the force of infection experienced by a susceptible individual in the space where the AQI was installed).
Assuming random allocation of AQIs to locations, at 20% coverage and 80% efficacy, annualized disease incidence decreased by `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "low_incidence"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "hi_incidence"), scale = 100)`% across `r endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "n_post")` stochastic simulations) for the SARS-CoV-2 pathogen and by `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "low_incidence"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "hi_incidence"), scale = 100)`%) for the influenza A/B pathogen (@fig-endemic, panels A and D).
Active infection prevalence declined by `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_prevalence_reduction"), scale = 100)`%, from `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_prevalence_baseline"), digits = 1, scale = 1)`% to `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_prevalence_post"), digits = 1, scale = 1)`% on average for SARS-CoV-2 and declined by `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_prevalence_reduction"), scale = 100)`%, from `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_prevalence_baseline"), digits = 1, scale = 1)`% to `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_prevalence_post"), digits = 1, scale = 1)`% for influenza A/B on average (@fig-endemic, panels B and E).
Increasing coverage or efficacy both led to larger reductions in infection incidence (@fig-endemic, panels C and F).
For example, keeping efficacy fixed at 80% and increasing coverage to 60%, reductions in annualized incidence were `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.6, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.6, "low_incidence"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.6, "hi_incidence"), scale = 100)`%) and `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.6, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.6, "low_incidence"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.6, "hi_incidence"), scale = 100)`%) for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A/B, respectively.
Similarly, fixing coverage at 20%, average reductions in annualized incidence were `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.4, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`%, `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.6, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% and `r format_result(endemic_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% for the SARS-CoV-2 pathogen at 40%, 60% and 80% assumed efficacy, respectively, and `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.4, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`%, `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.6, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% and `r format_result(endemic_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "mean_incidence_reduction"), scale = 100)`% for the influenza A/B pathogen.

**Projected AQI impact is larger for the influenza A/B archetype than for the SARS-CoV-2 archetype.**
Across all intervention scenarios explored, AQI installation produced greater proportional reductions in disease for the influenza A/B archetype than for the SARS-CoV-2 archetype (@fig-endemic).
Across equivalent coverage and efficacy levels ranging from 40% to 80%, reductions in annualized disease incidence for influenza A/B were `r format_result(endemic_ratio_range("mean_incidence_reduction")$low, scale = 1)`–`r format_result(endemic_ratio_range("mean_incidence_reduction")$high, scale = 1)`$\times$ higher than those observed for SARS-CoV-2.
Similarly, reductions in active infection prevalence were approximately `r format_result(endemic_ratio_range("mean_prevalence_reduction")$low, scale = 1)`–`r format_result(endemic_ratio_range("mean_prevalence_reduction")$high, scale = 1)`$\times$ higher for influenza A/B than for SARS-CoV-2 across the same range of coverage and efficacy.
These differences reflect the higher sensitivity of pathogens with lower $R_0$ and shorter generation times to reductions in per-contact transmission risk, suggesting that AQI installation would have particularly strong effects on influenza A/B endemic pathogens.

**Specifically targeting the highest-risk locations substantially increases the projected impact of AQI installation.**
Across all efficacy and coverage combinations explored, targeting installation of AQI to the highest-risk locations consistently produced greater reductions in infection incidence compared to scenarios where installation was done randomly (i.e. installed in locations irrespective of transmission risk) (@fig-targeting, panel A).
For example, at 20% coverage and 80% efficacy, targeting installation to highest-risk locations reduced annual incidence by an average of `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "max_value"), scale = 100)`%) for the SARS-CoV-2 archetype compared with `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "random"), scale = 100)`% under random installation (range `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "random", "incidence_reduction", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2, "random", "incidence_reduction", "max_value"), scale = 100)`%), a `r format_result(targeting_relative_increase("sars_cov_2", 0.8, 0.2), scale = 100)`% relative increase in impact (@fig-targeting, panel B).
Similar patterns were observed for the influenza A/B archetype, with targeted deployment achieving a `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "targeted_riskiness", "incidence_reduction", "max_value"), scale = 100)`%) reduction compared to the random installation achieving a `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.8, 0.2, "random"), scale = 100)`% reduction at equivalent coverage and efficacy, a `r format_result(targeting_relative_increase("flu", 0.8, 0.2), scale = 100)`% relative increase in impact (@fig-targeting, panel C).
In the model, targeting AQI installation to the highest-risk locations enables the same reduction in annualized incidence to be achieved with lower levels of overall coverage.
For example, for the SARS-CoV-2 archetype, a 30% reduction in annualized incidence required slightly above 60% AQI coverage under random implementation, while targeted coverage achieved the same reduction at only approximately 45% coverage (@fig-targeting, panel B).
This disparity was even more pronounced for the influenza A/B archetype – at 80% efficacy, a 30% reduction in annualized incidence was reached with only 20% targeted coverage, compared with 40% coverage when AQI installation was done at random.
A 50% reduction in infection incidence required approximately 40% targeted coverage versus approximately 60% random coverage (@fig-targeting, panel E).
These results indicate that, if the highest-risk locations can be accurately identified, targeting them can reduce the coverage required for equivalent population-level impact and substantially improve the efficiency of AQI deployment.

**Risk-based targeting provided the greatest relative benefit at low coverage levels.**
Across both pathogen archetypes, the relative benefit of targeting AQI installation based on riskiness (compared to random allocation) was greatest at low coverage levels and declined as coverage increased (and thus the two strategies converge; becoming identical when 100% of locations have AQI installed) (@fig-targeting, panels C and F).
At 20% coverage and 60% efficacy, the range of relative extra impact from targeting AQI installation was `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.6, 0.2, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%–`r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.6, 0.2, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "max_value"), scale = 100)`% for the SARS-CoV-2 archetype, and `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.6, 0.2, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%–`r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.6, 0.2, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "max_value"), scale = 100)`% for the influenza A/B archetype.
The benefit remained substantial at moderate coverage but diminished at higher levels, with relative extra impacts falling to `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.6, 0.8, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.6, 0.8, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(targeting_value("sars_cov_2", 0.6, 0.8, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "max_value"), scale = 100)`%) for SARS-CoV-2 and `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.6, 0.8, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.6, 0.8, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(targeting_value("flu", 0.6, 0.8, "targeted_vs_random", "rel_extra_impact", "max_value"), scale = 100)`%) for influenza A/B at 80% coverage and 60% efficacy.
This is due to the fact that as coverage increases, there is a greater overlap between locations selected by random and riskiness-based targeting.
The absolute difference in percentage reduction between random and targeted allocation strategies followed a similar pattern (@fig-targeting, panels D and G) peaking at mid-range coverage before converging at high coverages (as in these scenarios, most locations received AQIs).
These results indicate that targeting the highest-risk locations provides the largest proportional advantage when deployment resources are limited.

**AQI installation is also projected to substantially affect transmission dynamics and infection incidence in epidemic scenarios.**
Next, we evaluated the impact of AQIs on infection incidence across two archetypal epidemic scenarios, representing influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2 pathogens.
Across both epidemic archetypes, higher efficacy or wider coverage led to reductions in infection incidence across all metrics considered.
Without intervention, the peak incidence of the influenza A/B archetype was `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("flu", "peak_daily_incidence", "mean_value"))` per 1,000 (range `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("flu", "peak_daily_incidence", "min_value"))`-`r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("flu", "peak_daily_incidence", "max_value"))`) with a final epidemic size of `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% of total population (range `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "max_value"), scale = 100)`%), whereas the SARS-CoV-2 archetype yielded a peak incidence of `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("sars_cov_2", "peak_daily_incidence", "mean_value"))` per 1,000 (range `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("sars_cov_2", "peak_daily_incidence", "min_value"))`-`r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("sars_cov_2", "peak_daily_incidence", "max_value"))`) and a final epidemic size of `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("sars_cov_2", "epidemic_final_size", "mean_value"), scale = 100)`% of total population (range `r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("sars_cov_2", "epidemic_final_size", "min_value"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(epidemic_baseline_value("sars_cov_2", "epidemic_final_size", "max_value"), scale = 100)`%).
As with our results examining endemic scenarios, the impact of AQI installation was more pronounced in the influenza A/B archetype.
Random AQI installation at 40% coverage and 60% efficacy reduced the final epidemic size by `r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "mean_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "min_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "max_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`%), compared with only `r format_result(epidemic_value("sars_cov_2", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "mean_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`% (range `r format_result(epidemic_value("sars_cov_2", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "min_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`%-`r format_result(epidemic_value("sars_cov_2", "epidemic_final_size", "Random", 0.6, 0.4, "max_pct_reduction"), scale = 100)`%) for the SARS-CoV-2 archetype under the same settings (@fig-epidemic, panels A and E).

Increasing either efficacy or coverage yielded similar increases in the impact on epidemic peak and final size.
For the influenza A/B archetype, expanding randomly allocated coverage from 40% to 60% at 40% efficacy lowered the final epidemic size by `r format_result(epidemic_reduction(0.4, 0.6), scale = 100)`%, approximately matching the `r format_result(epidemic_reduction(0.6, 0.4), scale = 100)`% from instead increasing efficacy from 40% to 60% while holding coverage at 40% (@fig-epidemic, panel E).

As with our endemic scenario results, targeted AQI strategies achieved higher reductions in infection incidence at lower coverage levels than the random strategy.
For the influenza A/B archetype at 60% efficacy, the random strategy required 60% coverage to reach an average peak daily incidence of `r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "peak_daily_incidence", "Random", 0.6, 0.6))` per 1,000, while the targeted strategy achieved lower results with only 40% coverage, producing an average peak daily incidence of `r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "peak_daily_incidence", "Targeted", 0.6, 0.4))` per 1,000 (@fig-epidemic, panel G).
This pattern also held at lower coverage levels: the random strategy’s result at 40% coverage (average peak daily incidence of `r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "peak_daily_incidence", "Random", 0.6, 0.4))` per 1,000) was comparable to the targeted strategy’s outcome at just 20% coverage, where peak daily incidence was `r format_result(epidemic_value("flu", "peak_daily_incidence", "Targeted", 0.6, 0.2))` per 1,000 (@fig-epidemic, panel G).
In these cases, taking a targeted approach allowed a 20% reduction in the coverage required to achieve a given infection incidence reduction.

# Discussion

Our results highlight the potential impact that widespread improvements to indoor air quality (IAQ) could have on respiratory-virus transmission and associated disease burden.
Across the pathogen archetypes explored here, we highlight the potential for widespread introduction of AQIs to yield substantial reductions in endemic disease burden as coverage and efficacy increase, with larger gains when interventions are targeted to higher-risk locations rather than distributed at random.
In epidemic scenarios, AQIs are projected to reduce peak incidence and population-level spread.
Our modeled results suggest that AQIs of modest efficacy and floor-area coverage are unlikely to control pandemics driven by pathogens with moderate to high ${R}_{0}$ (e.g. above 1.5) on their own.
However, widespread presence of AQIs with the assumed efficacies could i) slow epidemic progression and spread, buying valuable time for countermeasure development, healthcare capacity surging, etc.; and ii) reduce the need for community-based mitigation measures (such as school or business closures) to control spread, which are typically highly costly from a socio-economic perspective.
These conclusions are consistent with current practice guidance that positions ventilation, filtration, and ultraviolet germicidal irradiation as foundational layers of protection, and with policy frameworks that formalize minimum performance targets for infectious-aerosol control [@who2021ventilation].
Taken together, our analyses suggest that interventions improving indoor air could support burden reduction while underscoring that realized impact will hinge on real-world effectiveness, coverage, targeting, maintenance, and other factors relating to their practical deployment [@okokon2025the].

In our endemic simulations, reductions in infection incidence scale with both coverage and assumed efficacy of AQIs, with larger absolute and relative effects for the influenza A/B archetype modeled than for the SARS-CoV-2 archetype.
Near the epidemic threshold of $R\ =\ 1$, standard epidemic theory implies strongly non-linear behaviour, with small proportional reductions in transmission translating into disproportionately large changes in equilibrium incidence and prevalence when the pathogen reproduction number is closer to this threshold [@rohani2011modeling; @kermack1927a].
Baseline reproduction numbers for seasonal and pandemic influenza typically lie closer to the epidemic threshold of $R\ =\ 1$ (typically between 1.2 and 1.4 for seasonal influenza [@biggerstaff2014estimates]), whereas early SARS-CoV-2 estimates were higher (often $R\ >\ 2.5$) [@liu2020the]; a difference which we captured in the way we parameterised the pathogen archetypes presented here.
As $R_0$ and the generation interval varied simultaneously between our two pathogen archetypes, we did not disentangle their respective contributions to the observed difference in intervention impact.
For example, coverage of 40% of non-household floor area with AQIs with efficacy 60% led to 26.2% and 10.2% reductions in annual infection incidence for influenza A/B and SARS-CoV-2 pathogens, respectively.
Crucially, because overall annual infection incidence for our SARS-CoV-2 pathogen is higher, this still translates into sizeable reductions in absolute burden, even though it remains a (relatively) smaller fraction of total burden.
In both cases, achieving substantial impact (e.g. \>30% reduction) was contingent on comparatively high levels of coverage and/or efficacy: to achieve 30% reduction at assumed 60% efficacy required approximately 90% and approximately 45% coverage for the SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A/B pathogens, respectively.

In our modeled epidemic scenarios, installed AQIs reduced the final epidemic size and peak incidence with more pronounced effects again for the influenza A/B archetype than for SARS-CoV-2 scenarios.
Our modeled results show that AQIs of modest efficacy and floor-area coverage are unlikely to achieve containment of the most highly transmissible pathogens on their own.
However, these results also indicate that these measures could still play a role in both reducing and slowing epidemic growth and associated population-level spread, buying time for the development of countermeasures under accelerated (but still delayed relative to epidemic onset) timelines, as with the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness’ 100 Days Mission.
Moreover, by lowering baseline transmission in public and community venues, IAQ improvements may also reduce reliance on disruptive measures such as prolonged school or business closures, which carry documented and persistent educational and macroeconomic costs [@oecd2020learning; @haw2022optimizing; @rothwell2024global].
Together, these results position clean indoor air as a supportive component of layered epidemic control, even if not a standalone panacea for it.

Despite these promising results, an important limitation of the analyses presented here is that sizeable and reliable reductions in disease burden arise most clearly at high coverage (typically \>30% of eligible non-household floor area).
Widespread and comprehensive improvement of indoor air quality across such a large stock of buildings is likely to be very expensive, and whether such levels can be achieved (especially in the short-term) remains an important practical question that we do not address here.
It is important to note, however, that the costs of different AQI technologies remain deeply uncertain (and likely highly variable), and no rigorous cost-effectiveness analysis has yet compared AQI interventions to alternative disease control measures (such as population-level vaccination).
Without such analyses, whether AQI investments compare favourably to the per-person costs of other population-level control measures (such as vaccinating a comparable population fraction) remains an open question.
Irrespective, maximizing AQI impact for a given coverage level or budget is likely to remain crucial.
Our results indicate that targeting IAQ interventions to locations that contribute disproportionately to onward transmission yields larger population-level benefits than random allocation at the same coverage, with the advantage of targeting greatest when coverage is low and diminishing as coverage approaches saturation.
This pattern is consistent with previous theoretical work highlighting that strategic allocation of general transmission reducing measures outperforms random allocation and that the two converge only at very high coverage [@tanaka2014random; @hadjichrysanthou2015epidemic], as well as empirical evidence that a minority of venues account for a large share of infections [@chang2021mobility] and that transmission is highly overdispersed [@sneppen2021overdispersion; @wegehaupt2023superspreading].

Our projections suggest that targeted allocation of IAQ interventions to the highest-risk locations could enable greater impact even at lower levels of coverage; but consistently and comprehensively identifying these highest-risk locations remains challenging.
The exact location in which infection occurs is not typically observed and difficult to identify via traditional contact-tracing based methods, especially in the context of asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic transmission (as for COVID-19 [@he2020temporal; @johansson2021sarscov]) and constraints on the resourcing of contact tracing infrastructure [@lash2021covid].
Additionally, transmission risk is strongly context dependent: beyond ventilation (which we use as a proxy for risk in the analyses presented here and which represents an important limitation of our work), factors such as occupancy, duration of co-presence, vocalization and activity intensity shape emission and exposure [@wang2021airborne; @qian2021indoor].
Resolving patterns of transmission and risk at finer spatial granularity is therefore crucial.
Previous work has highlighted the promise of digital contact tracing as a way to provide time-stamped proximity records that strengthen case–context linkage when recall is incomplete and exposure windows span multiple venues [@kendall2023epidemiological].
Similarly, previous work has highlighted that aggregated mobile network data can quantify venue-level person-time and crowding from anonymized device movements to estimate setting-specific exposure and risk [@chang2021mobility].
More broadly, scalable sensing systems for proxies of poor ventilation and thus high transmission risk (such as CO$_2$) could also comprehensively characterize ventilation across locations and identification of persistently under-ventilated spaces [@peng2021exhaled; @rudnick2003risk].

Indeed, a major limitation of this work is the simplified representation of the physical spaces that individuals visit and the contact structures they form within them.
Although we differentiate setting types and locations and parameterize their relative contributions using estimates derived from previous work [@ferguson2005strategies], each location is represented as a single unit, without separate rooms, movement between them, or any representation of airflow.
We therefore do not capture the contact structures that arise from realistic daily schedules, differences in dwell times, and repeated encounters within and between rooms.
For example, children are represented as a single age group, and we do not distinguish primary school pupils remaining in one classroom from secondary school pupils moving between classrooms and mixing with different classmates.
Future extensions could represent individual rooms and distinguish more age groups.
Time-use data, such as the American Time Use Survey [@hamermesh2005data], or mobility network data could inform schedules and dwell times, allowing a more realistic representation of non-household transmission opportunities.

We also do not explicitly differentiate shorter-range, droplet-mediated transmission (more closely determined by the specific interpersonal contacts made within a location or particular room) from longer-range aerosol inhalation, which depends more on room airflows and ventilation [@wang2021airborne].
Instead, we represent AQI effects via fixed efficacies that implicitly combine both the intrinsic performance of the intervention and the proportion of total transmission that is avertible by air-quality modification.
The comparative contributions of these different pathways currently remain poorly resolved, and evidence suggests that relative contribution may vary across pathogens and contexts.
Infectious influenza virus has been detected in fine exhaled aerosols from symptomatic cases [@yan2018infectious] and infectious SARS-CoV-2 aerosols have been shown to be emitted by COVID-19 patients [@hawks2021infectious].
For RSV however, aerosol spread has been demonstrated experimentally but remains less well characterized than droplet and contact routes [@kulkarni2016evidence].
Better resolving these distinct mechanisms and integrating them into the same framework would be a valuable direction for future work.

A related limitation concerns our representation of within-room transmission dynamics.
Although our framework advances prior individual-based models by explicitly linking setting-level ventilation and riskiness to exposure via a Wells-Riley-based mechanism [@szeto2010review], the indoor-air calculations used for parameterisation assume a steady-state, well-mixed approximation for each location that fails to capture fine-scale within-location granularity in airflow dynamics and spread of exhaled infectious virus throughout the space [@edwards2024the].
We also neglect inter-room airflows and building-scale transport, representing between-location variation through stochastic heterogeneity in overall transmission risk rather than explicitly coupling that altered risk to changes or differences in airflow.
These simplifications were chosen for computational tractability at population scale, but they omit mechanisms that can materially influence risk in specific spaces [@noakes2009mathematical; @mukherjee2022a].
Further refining our current representation of indoor space and adding more realistic spatial structure and airflow within a particular location, such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models with our existing IBM would be valuable.

Another limitation is that we do not represent specific AQI technologies or undertake health-economic evaluations, limiting our ability to assess the cost-effectiveness of interventions aiming to improve IAQ.
This choice reflects the present evidence base: randomized and quasi-experimental studies of venue-level AQIs remain limited in number, heterogeneous in design, and mixed in outcomes.
For example, trials in aged-care facilities showed no clear reduction in acute respiratory infections with in-room HEPA filtration and only modest, aggregate effects with germicidal UV in long-term care [@thottiyilsultanmuhammedabdulkhadar2024air; @shoubridge2025germicidal], while reviews underscore sparse transmission-endpoint data and variable implementation quality [@okokon2025the].
Formal cost-effectiveness evidence is similarly limited: some analyses during the COVID-19 period suggest circumstances where portable filtration or ventilation upgrades could be cost-effective, but these findings depend on assumptions about device performance, usage patterns, energy costs, and background incidence that vary widely across settings [@zafari2022the; @chang2023a].
Rigorous evaluation of comparative effectiveness remains a priority, but is methodologically challenging: trial design is complicated by the need for large sample sizes, because individuals typically spend only a fraction of their infectious period in any single trial venue, so venue-specific interventions act on only a limited share of exposure; this dilutes detectable effects and increases required sample sizes; a feature that is further complicated by the possibility of averted infections occurring via other routes, in other locations individuals visit where IAQ interventions are not installed.
Generating such evidence is therefore crucial.
Integrating it into population-level models of spread and epidemiological impact will facilitate rigorous cost-effectiveness analyses across payer perspectives (societal, health-system, building owner or operator, employer or school district, etc.), decision contexts (e.g. time horizon, discounting choices etc.), and co-benefits (such as reduced PM$_{2.5}$ exposure and productivity or attendance gains).

Despite these limitations, our work projects substantial potential burden reductions from improving indoor air quality at scale, across both endemic and epidemic contexts, conditional on the assumed intervention efficacies.
Realizing these benefits will depend on real-world effectiveness, implementation quality and coverage across diverse building stocks, sustained operation and maintenance, and alignment with performance-based standards that specify equivalent clean air delivery and infection-risk management modes.
It will also require practical guidance and workforce capacity to assess and upgrade ventilation, filtration, and air disinfection in priority settings.
Further research should quantify real-world effectiveness for specific technologies in varied venues, generate comparative- and cost-effectiveness evidence across payer perspectives, and develop measurement systems that resolve venue-level risk in near-real time.
